metadata.historical_target: Sirmium / modern Sremska Mitrovica, around 379 CE
metadata.certainty_rule: No exact proclamation building, room, platform, or 379 city plan is certified by these sources.

geography.summary: Roman Sirmium lies beneath/within modern Sremska Mitrovica on the north (left) bank of the Sava, with the Bosut joining the Sava nearby. Archaeological sources place the palatial district in the southeastern part of the Roman city beside the Sava; a circus/hippodrome is adjacent and its orientation shaped neighboring buildings. The urban footprint and river margins changed over time, and the modern built environment obscures most remains.

findings: A peer-reviewed article describes Sirmium/Mitrovica at the contact between a diluvial terrace and the Sava inundation plain. It says the terrace projects to the Sava channel, narrowing the alluvial plain at this crossing, and its relative height gave more flood safety than surrounding ground.
The same article describes marshy alluvial plain on three sides, with active streams and Sava oxbows; it mentions two historical river islands/aîts near Sirmium, Cassia and Carbonaria.

The Institute of Archaeology page independently describes marshes on the west/north/east sides of the urban core and the Čikas stream east of the city. It describes the city beneath modern Sremska Mitrovica on the Sava.

These establish a floodplain/terrace setting, not exact 379 shoreline, water mask, ford/bridge location, season-specific flooding, or the state of channels in a particular year. River regulation, drainage, infill, settlement deposits, and modern construction make present-day empty map space insufficient evidence for ancient dry land.
landform_and_water.extrapolation_limit: The 2019 geomorphology article focuses on Lower Posavina medieval urbanization, though its Sirmium passage discusses landform and ancient-era contextual information. Apply its broad geomorphology cautiously; it does not reconstruct 4th-century hydrology at parcel scale.

archaeological_phases_relevant_to_379: Institute of Archaeology: Sirmium was beneath modern Sremska Mitrovica; system research began in 1957. The inner core estimate of about 66 ha is inferred from find positions of ramparts. Palace complex is over 6 ha, only partly explored; its position/orientation and circus influenced surrounding buildings.

Vojvodina Tourism Organization: the palace complex was built in the late 3rd / early 4th century in the southeastern elite district along the Sava. The circus was discovered adjacent to the palace and helped identify the palatial site; the exposed portion is only part of it, with multiple repair/mosaic layers indicating long use and changes.

Archive of Vojvodina article: reports damage/repairs to the rampart after the Quadi incursion in the 370s, with a later south-wall layer containing a coin of Theodosius dated 379–395; it discusses burnt destruction deposits at central sites with coin termini 383–392. These are archaeological horizons and interpretations, not a complete, securely dated snapshot for 379.

Archive article says Sirmium and Pannonia came under Gothic control somewhat after 380, while acknowledging uncertainty from scarce sources; avoid turning that phrasing into a precise event-date claim for 379.
geography.proclamation_site_limit: The sources support Sirmium as an imperial residence/major late Roman center and support a palace-circus complex. They do not certify that an accession/proclamation in 379 occurred in a particular palace room, circus box, gate, or other mapped structure. The city's broad gazetteer point and modern visitor-site coordinates cannot supply that missing evidence.
geography.plan_limit: No 379 plan, exact shoreline, exact palace perimeter, exact circus footprint from this dossier, or comprehensive old-city wall polygon is asserted. Excavation has exposed only parts of a heavily built-over site; local map points are anchors with different meanings and scales.

sources_read.title: Natural Conditions as a Factor of Urbanization of the Lower Posavina in the Middle Ages
sources_read.author: Dejana Vasin
sources_read.publisher: Istraživanja / Journal of Historical Researches 30 (2019), pp. 45–68; DOI 10.19090/i.2019.30.45-68
sources_read.passages_read: Collector read selected geomorphology; architect directly checked physical PDF13–14, printed57–58: terrace–inundation contact and continuation on relative flood safety, marshes, active streams and oxbows. Other collector sections remain separately attributed, not a whole-paper reading by root.
sources_read.use_and_limit: Peer-reviewed article whose main scope is medieval urbanization; its landform discussion is useful at broad scale and references ancient features, but cannot fix Roman-era microtopography, waterline, or a 379 scene.
